title: Do Patients Feel More Capable of Managing Their Own Health After Psychiatric Treatment? A Narrative Review of Patient Activation, Empowerment, Self-Management, and Recovery
content: Psychiatric treatment is conventionally judged by symptom reduction and service use, yet recovery-oriented policy asks a different question: does treatment leave people more capable of managing their own health? This narrative review synthesises evidence on patient activation, empowerment, self-efficacy, illness self-management and personal recovery to determine whether, and under what conditions, people report greater capability after mental health care. Capability proved measurable, mutable and clinically meaningful: activation predicts self-management, medication adherence, quality of life and readmission, and is largely independent of sociodemographic characteristics. Self-management interventions in severe mental illness improve hope, empowerment, self-efficacy and self-rated recovery. Peer support yields small but consistent gains in empowerment and personal recovery (g = 0.15) without reliable effects on symptoms or service use; recovery colleges improve self-confidence and self-understanding but lack randomised evidence; and Illness Management and Recovery shows inconsistent effects that track participation. Shared decision-making, conversational feedback of patient-reported outcomes and facilitated psychiatric advance directives strengthen autonomy, the last roughly halving the likelihood of coercive crisis intervention. Internalised stigma, perceived coercion and clinician-dominated communication erode capability. The answer to the review question is a qualified yes: capability gains are reliable on person-centred outcomes when treatment deliberately targets them, but they are not an automatic by-product of symptom-focused care. Community mental health services should measure capability directly, train clinicians in collaborative communication and treat empowerment as an explicit clinical target.
